segments.t: At a major Paris radio station, acclaimed director Sacha Hartman gives a live broadcast interview about his provocative film. Camille waits patiently in the sound booth to escort the guest director back to the agency. Listen to the scene in French first.
Bonjour, Sacha Hartman.
Merci d'être avec nous.
Vous parlez un français parfait.
J'ai fréquenté l'école française à Berlin.
Mes parents ont toujours aimé la France.
Votre premier film a remporté un prix.
La Palme d'Or à Cannes!
Une association cherche à faire interdire votre film.
Comment réagissez-vous à ces attaques?
Je ne veux pas leur offrir une tribune.
Ni leur accorder la moindre attention.
Ils appartiennent à l'ancien monde.
L'interview est terminée, Sacha.
Nous devons y aller maintenant.
D'accord, je te suis.
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
Bonjour, Sacha Hartman.
'Hello, Sacha Hartman.' Radio hosts greet studio guests by full name after 'good day', setting a crisp broadcast tone in French.
Merci d'être avec nous.
'Thank you for being with us.' Thanking someone 'for doing' something links 'thanks' with 'of' plus the base action rather than 'for' plus '-ing' as in English.
Vous parlez un français parfait.
'You speak perfect French.' Language names stay lowercase in French, and adding 'a' before 'French perfect' praises the quality of someone's speech.
J'ai fréquenté l'école française à Berlin.
'I attended the French school in Berlin.' Watch the cognate 'frequented': it is what you'd say in French for 'attended' a school.
Mes parents ont toujours aimé la France.
'My parents have always loved France.' Country names keep 'the' in French even after 'love', unlike English where 'France' stands bare.
Votre premier film a remporté un prix.
'Your first movie won a prize.' Built from 'carry back', the action pictures taking home a trophy, while the final word can mean both 'prize' and 'price'.
La Palme d'Or à Cannes!
'The Golden Palm at Cannes!' Linking 'palm' to 'gold' with 'of' tells what material Cannes's famous festival trophy is made of in French.
Une association cherche à faire interdire votre film.
'An association is trying to ban your film.' Stringing together 'seeks to make forbid' expresses 'trying to have your film banned' in French.
Comment réagissez-vous à ces attaques?
'How do you react to these attacks?' Flipping 'react' and polite 'you' after 'how' gives the presenter's question formal broadcast polish.
Je ne veux pas leur offrir une tribune.
'I do not want to give them a platform.' Notice 'to them' sits ahead of 'offer', and the final word originally means a speaker's rostrum in French.
Ni leur accorder la moindre attention.
'Nor give them the slightest attention.' Opening with 'nor' extends Sacha's refusal in the negative, followed by an expression meaning 'the least attention'.
Ils appartiennent à l'ancien monde.
'They belong to the old world.' Placed ahead of 'world', that describing word means 'former' or 'bygone', whereas after 'world' in French it would mean 'ancient'.
L'interview est terminée, Sacha.
'The interview is over, Sacha.' French borrows 'interview' straight from English for media broadcasts, pairing it with a cognate meaning 'terminated' or 'finished'.
Nous devons y aller maintenant.
'We must go now.' Slipping 'there' ahead of 'go' is standard in French whenever 'go' has no destination named after it.
D'accord, je te suis.

'All right, I am following you.' Look closely at a famous twin form in French: 'I follow' and 'I am' look and sound identical, though 'you' before it proves Sacha means 'follow'. Now let's listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.
Bonjour, Sacha Hartman.
Merci d'être avec nous.
Vous parlez un français parfait.
J'ai fréquenté l'école française à Berlin.
Mes parents ont toujours aimé la France.
Votre premier film a remporté un prix.
La Palme d'Or à Cannes!
Une association cherche à faire interdire votre film.
Comment réagissez-vous à ces attaques?
Je ne veux pas leur offrir une tribune.
Ni leur accorder la moindre attention.
Ils appartiennent à l'ancien monde.
L'interview est terminée, Sacha.
Nous devons y aller maintenant.
D'accord, je te suis.
As Sacha Hartman wraps up his defiant interview, Camille must quickly guide him outside through brewing street protests. See you next time!
À bientôt!
